analogy.p: Imagine a tug of war with two equal teams. Team Gravity pulls inwards and Team Pressure (from fusion energy) pulls outwards. While the teams are equal the rope does not move, just as a main sequence star keeps a steady size. When Team Pressure's energy supply (hydrogen fuel) runs out, Team Gravity starts to win and the star changes: the core shrinks, and the outer layers swell as a red giant. The analogy breaks down because a real star's balance corrects itself automatically (if the star shrinks, fusion speeds up and pushes back), whereas a rope team does not.
analogy.t: A star as a perfectly balanced tug of war

bullets: Know the **order of the stages** exactly. Mark schemes award a mark for each stage in the right sequence, so a wrong order loses marks even if every stage is named.
Know **what causes each change**, not just the names. The recurring reason is a change in the balance between **gravity (inwards)** and **outward pressure from fusion energy**.
Know the **two routes** after the main sequence: red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf for Sun-sized stars; red supergiant, supernova, then neutron star or black hole for much more massive stars.
Know that **fusion in stars produced all the naturally occurring elements** and that **supernovae distribute them** through the universe.
Expect questions that ask you to **describe**, **explain** (give reasons) and **compare** life cycles, often worth 4 or 6 marks, plus short 1 to 2 mark recall questions.

This point links to **nuclear fusion** (4.4 Atomic structure), **gravity and forces**, **energy transfer by radiation**, and the **Big Bang** (hydrogen and helium formed early; heavier elements later in stars).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point covers **our Sun and Solar system** and **the life cycle of a star**. For the Solar system you need to know what it contains and how it fits inside a galaxy. For stars you need the whole story in the correct order: a **nebula** (cloud of dust and gas) is pulled together by **gravity** to form a **protostar**, which becomes a **main sequence star** when **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen begins, then changes when the fuel runs out. The ending depends on the star's **mass**, so you must be able to describe two routes, one for stars about the size of the Sun and one for much more massive stars. It is Physics only (triple science), so it appears on Paper 2 for those students.

bullets: The order of size from smallest to largest is: **moon or planet, then Solar system, then galaxy, then universe**.
A **star** makes its own light by fusion. Planets, moons and most other objects only **reflect** sunlight, so they are visible because of light from the Sun.
The Solar system formed from a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by **gravity**; most of the mass ended up in the centre and became the Sun, and the rest formed the other bodies.
Gravity from the huge mass of the Sun is the force that keeps everything in the Solar system **in orbit** around it.
The average distance from the Sun to the Earth is about **1.5 x 10^11 m** (150 million km). This is a useful number for speed = distance / time questions.
The Milky Way is a **spiral galaxy**; the Sun is in one of its outer regions, nowhere near the centre.
Link: how orbits work is covered in the next spec point, **orbital motion, natural and artificial satellites**.
core.h: Our Sun, the Milky Way and the Solar system
core.p: The **Sun** is a **star**: a huge ball of hot gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, that gives out its own light and heat because **nuclear fusion** happens in its core. Our Sun is just one of billions of stars in the **Milky Way galaxy**, and a **galaxy** is a very large collection of billions of stars held together by gravity. The **Solar system** is the Sun together with everything that orbits it, and it sits inside the Milky Way, which in turn is one galaxy among very many in the **universe**. Keeping the size order straight (planet, Solar system, galaxy, universe) is a common 1-mark question.

bullets: **Planets** (in order outwards from the Sun): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. A common memory phrase is 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming'.
**Dwarf planets** (for example Pluto and Ceres) orbit the Sun but are smaller than the planets and have not cleared other debris from the region around their orbit.
**Moons** are **natural satellites**: they orbit planets. Earth has one Moon; some planets have many.
**Asteroids** are rocky objects that orbit the Sun. Many are found in the **asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter**.
**Comets** are lumps of ice and dust that orbit the Sun in very stretched (elliptical) orbits, with a tail developing as they get close to the Sun.
Planets are held in orbit by **gravity**, not by any physical connection to the Sun.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are **rocky**; Jupiter and Saturn are **gas giants**; Uranus and Neptune are often called **ice giants**.
core.h: What is in the Solar system
core.p: The Solar system contains the **Sun** at the centre, **eight planets**, **dwarf planets**, the **natural satellites (moons)** of planets, **asteroids** and **comets**. The planets travel around the Sun in nearly circular orbits, while moons orbit planets. Everything in the system is held in orbit by the gravitational attraction of the Sun, and moons are held in orbit around their planets by the planet's gravity. You should be able to name and describe these objects.

bullets: A **nebula** is a cloud of dust and gas. The key word for the cause of collapse is **gravity**: the particles are attracted to each other.
As the cloud contracts, **temperature and density rise** because gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy of the particles.
A **protostar** is the hot dense core formed from the collapsing cloud before fusion begins.
Collapse continues until the **temperature and pressure in the core are high enough for nuclear fusion** to start.
Typical exam wording: 'the dust and gas are pulled together by **gravitational attraction** to form a protostar'. The words 'gravity' and 'dust and gas' are both worth looking for.
Several stars can form from the same nebula at the same time, which is why stars are often found in clusters.
Common error: saying that the protostar is 'on fire'. Nothing is burning; the heating comes from contraction under gravity.
core.h: How a star forms: nebula to protostar
core.p: All stars begin life in a **nebula**, which is a huge cloud of **dust and gas** (mostly hydrogen). Because the particles in the cloud attract each other through **gravity**, the cloud slowly clumps together and pulls inwards, and denser regions pull in more material. As the material falls inwards, gravitational potential energy is transferred to **thermal energy**, so the clump gets hotter and hotter. The dense, hot ball formed at this stage is called a **protostar**. It is not yet a proper star because fusion has not started.

bullets: Definition: fusion = **two light nuclei join to make a heavier nucleus** and energy is released.
Need: **very high temperature** (so nuclei have enough kinetic energy to overcome electrostatic repulsion) and **very high pressure** (so nuclei are close together and collide often).
In the Sun the main fusion reaction turns **hydrogen nuclei into helium nuclei**.
The energy released as radiation is what makes the star **shine**, and the thermal energy produced also keeps the core hot.
Fusion is different from **fission**, which is the splitting of a large unstable nucleus. Stars use fusion, nuclear power stations use fission.
Fusion of light elements releases energy up to **iron**. Making nuclei heavier than iron needs a net energy input, which is why they form in a supernova.
Link to 4.4: fusion is covered in the atomic structure topic as the joining of nuclei with a loss of some mass.
core.h: Nuclear fusion: what it is and why it needs extreme conditions
core.p: **Nuclear fusion** is the process in which **two light nuclei join together to form a heavier nucleus**. In stars, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium. In this process **some of the mass is converted into energy**, which is released as **radiation** (electromagnetic waves) and as kinetic energy of particles. Nuclei are positively charged, so they strongly **repel** each other. To get close enough to fuse, they must be moving extremely fast, which means the temperature must be extremely high, and they must also be squeezed close together at high pressure. This is why fusion only happens deep inside stars.

bullets: A main sequence star is stable because **the inward force of gravity equals the outward pressure caused by the energy released from fusion**.

If a star started to shrink, the core would heat up and fuse faster, increasing the outward pressure and pushing the star back to equilibrium. If it expanded, fusion would slow and gravity would pull it back. The balance is **self-correcting**.
This is a **long** stage because there is a huge supply of hydrogen fuel. The Sun's main sequence life is roughly 10 billion years in total.
**More massive stars use their fuel faster**, so they spend a shorter time on the main sequence than smaller stars.
Energy is released from the star as **electromagnetic radiation**, including visible light, infrared and ultraviolet.
Good phrase for 'explain why a star is stable': 'the **inward force due to gravity** is balanced by the **outward force due to the pressure of the hot gas produced by fusion**'.
The size of the Sun is roughly constant for billions of years because of this balance.
core.h: The main sequence: a long, stable phase
core.p: When fusion of hydrogen into helium begins in the core, the protostar becomes a **main sequence star**. This is the longest stage in a star's life, lasting billions of years. The star is **stable** because there is a balance of forces: **gravity pulls the outer layers inwards**, but the huge amount of energy released by fusion produces **outward pressure** (the hot gas tries to expand). When these two effects are equal the star neither shrinks nor expands. Our Sun is currently in this stage, and it has been stable for around 4.6 billion years and is expected to stay stable for billions more.

bullets: Trigger for leaving the main sequence: **hydrogen fuel in the core is running out**.
Outer layers **swell up** and the surface **cools**, so the star appears **red** (cooler surface means more red light).
In red giants and supergiants **helium and then heavier elements** are fused in the core and shells around it.
Fusion in stars can make elements **up to iron**. Each new element needs a higher temperature, which is why only the most massive stars go the whole way.
**Red giant** = star about the size of the Sun (or smaller). **Red supergiant** = star much larger than the Sun.
The Sun will become a red giant in about 5 billion years, and it will expand enough to swallow the inner planets.
Do not say the star 'burns hydrogen' as in a fire. Use **fuses**.
core.h: The end of the main sequence: red giant or red supergiant
core.p: After billions of years the **hydrogen in the core begins to run out**, so fusion of hydrogen slows and the outward pressure falls. Gravity now wins and the core is squeezed, which makes it hotter. The hotter core can fuse **helium** and then heavier elements, and the extra energy makes the outer layers **expand and cool**. The star becomes a **red giant** if it is about the size of the Sun or smaller, or a **red supergiant** if it is much larger than the Sun. They look red because the swollen outer surface is cooler than a main sequence star.

bullets: Sequence: main sequence, **red giant**, **white dwarf**, **black dwarf**.
A white dwarf is **small, very dense and hot**, and it is no longer fusing, so it gradually radiates energy away.
A **black dwarf** is a cold, dark remnant that no longer emits significant light.
This route applies to stars **similar to or smaller than the Sun**. Nothing in this route involves a supernova.
The Sun will follow this route: it will **not** explode as a supernova and it will **not** become a black hole.
Exam trap: 'dwarf' here refers to the small size of the remnant, not to a dwarf planet.
The time needed to cool is longer than the present age of the universe, so black dwarfs are predicted but not yet observed.
core.h: The fate of Sun-sized stars: white dwarf and black dwarf
core.p: A star about the size of the Sun (or smaller) does not have enough mass to fuse the heaviest elements. After the red giant phase it **loses its outer layers**, leaving a hot, dense core that is a **white dwarf**. A white dwarf is small, hot and white and no longer produces energy by fusion, so it slowly **cools down**, eventually fading to a cold, dark **black dwarf**. It takes extremely long for white dwarfs to cool, so no black dwarfs are thought to exist yet.

bullets: Sequence: main sequence, **red supergiant**, **supernova**, then **neutron star or black hole**.
A **supernova** is a massive explosion that happens when a very massive star at the end of its life collapses and its outer layers are thrown off.
The core left behind is a **neutron star** if it is not too massive, or a **black hole** if it is massive enough.
A **black hole** has such strong gravity that **nothing, not even light, can escape** once it passes the boundary.
Elements **heavier than iron** are produced in the supernova explosion, which is why the explosion is so important to the origin of the elements.
The explosion scatters dust and gas into space, which can later become **new nebulae** and form new stars and planets.
Compare with Sun-sized stars: the massive route involves **supernova** and ends as a **neutron star or black hole**; the small route ends as **white dwarf then black dwarf**.
core.h: The fate of massive stars: supernova, neutron star or black hole
core.p: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a **red supergiant**, which can fuse elements all the way up to **iron**. Once the core is iron, no more energy can be released by fusion, so the core collapses suddenly under gravity. The collapse triggers a huge explosion called a **supernova**, which blows the outer layers into space and releases enough energy to create elements **heavier than iron**. What is left of the core depends on the mass: it forms a **neutron star** (extremely dense, made mostly of neutrons), or, for the most massive stars, a **black hole**. A black hole's gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

bullets: **Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.** This sentence is almost word for word what the spec says.
**Supernovae spread these elements through the universe**, so new stars and planets can contain them.
The Sun is therefore a **second-generation star**: it formed from the remains of earlier stars, which is why the Earth contains heavy elements.
Fusion in ordinary stars releases energy while building elements up to iron. Heavier elements need extra energy, available in a supernova.
The atoms in your body (carbon, oxygen, calcium and so on) were made in stars, so you are made of 'star material'.
The cycle is: **nebula, star, supernova, new nebula, new stars and planets**, shown in the recycling diagram.
Link: Big Bang theory (4.8.2) explains the origin of hydrogen and helium; stellar fusion and supernovae explain the rest.
core.h: Where the chemical elements come from
core.p: Immediately after the Big Bang the universe was made almost entirely of the lightest elements, **hydrogen** and **helium**. All the other **naturally occurring elements** were made later by **nuclear fusion inside stars**, where nuclei are joined to form heavier ones as the star ages. Elements **heavier than iron** form in the extreme conditions of a **supernova**. When massive stars explode as supernovae, these elements are **distributed throughout the universe** in the dust and gas, and later become part of new nebulae. Because our Solar system contains elements heavier than hydrogen and helium (such as carbon, oxygen and iron in the Earth and in our bodies), the Sun and planets must have formed from material that came from earlier stars.

bullets: **Sun-sized or smaller:** red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf. Long main sequence life.
**Much more massive than the Sun:** red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole. Shorter main sequence life.
More mass means stronger gravity, so the core is hotter and fuses **more heavy elements**.
Only massive stars reach the iron stage that triggers a supernova.
Whether a massive star leaves a neutron star or black hole depends on how much mass is left in the core.
In an exam: always state which route you are describing, e.g. 'a star much more massive than the Sun...'.
Common comparison marks: 'red supergiant instead of red giant', 'supernova', 'neutron star or black hole instead of white dwarf'.
core.h: Why mass decides a star's fate
core.p: A star's mass at birth determines its **temperature, how fast it uses fuel, how long it lives and how it ends**. A larger mass means stronger gravity compressing the core, so the core reaches higher temperature and pressure and fuses elements further up the periodic table. Massive stars therefore use their fuel quickly and have **shorter lives**, ending in a supernova, while smaller stars live much longer and end quietly as white dwarfs. Everything in the two routes can be traced back to mass.

bullets: **Nebula to protostar:** gravity pulls the cloud together; gravitational potential energy is transferred to thermal energy.
**Protostar to main sequence:** fusion starts once the core is hot and dense enough, creating outward pressure.
**Main sequence:** gravity (in) = pressure (out). Stable.
**End of fuel:** fusion falls, gravity (in) is greater than pressure (out) in the core, so the core shrinks and heats, and the outer layers expand.
**Massive star iron core:** fusion can no longer release energy, so gravity wins decisively and the core collapses, causing a supernova.
**Remnants:** white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes are held together by their own gravity but no longer fuse hydrogen.
Energy transfer: gravitational potential energy to thermal energy to radiation: this links to the **energy stores and transfers** topic.
core.h: Forces and energy: linking the whole life cycle
core.p: Every change in the life cycle is a story of **gravity versus outward pressure**. In the nebula, gravity wins and the cloud collapses. In the main sequence, the forces balance. When the fuel runs low, gravity wins again in the core, which heats it and swells the outer layers. At the end of a massive star's life, gravity wins so completely that the core collapses. Seeing the pattern makes the sequence easy to remember and gives you the reason for 'explain' questions.

bullets: For ordering questions, write the stages as a chain with arrows in your rough work, then copy it out: **nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf**.
For the massive route write: **nebula, protostar, main sequence, red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole**.
Two stars that begin in the same place diverge **after the main sequence**. Mark the branching point on any flow chart.
Mass-ordering questions: more massive means shorter life and ending with supernova.
Calculation links: speed = distance / time for light travel from the Sun (distance 1.5 x 10^11 m, speed of light 3.0 x 10^8 m/s gives about 500 s).
Always use the words **fusion**, **gravity** and **pressure** in explanations; examiners look for them.
core.p: Questions on this topic usually test whether you can **put stages in order**, **choose the right route for a given mass**, and **give a reason for a change**. Diagrams of the life cycle may be given with blanks or labels to fill in, and you may be asked to complete a flow chart. Practise writing short, precise causal sentences using the pattern 'because... gravity... pressure... fusion...'.

bullets: **Atomic structure (4.4):** fusion is the joining of nuclei; compare with fission.
**Energy (4.1):** the Sun's energy reaches us as radiation; gravitational potential energy changes to thermal energy during collapse.
**Forces (4.5):** gravity is a non-contact force; its strength depends on mass and distance.
**Electromagnetic waves (4.6):** stars emit radiation across the spectrum; hotter objects emit more at shorter wavelengths.
**Chemistry:** the periodic table's elements beyond hydrogen and helium exist because of stellar fusion and supernovae.
**Red-shift and the Big Bang (next spec points):** hydrogen and helium come from the early universe; heavier elements come from stars.
core.h: Link to other topics and common extensions
core.p: Space physics ties together several other parts of the course. Fusion links to atomic structure, orbits link to forces, and the origin of the elements links to chemistry and the periodic table. Knowing these links helps with synoptic and application questions that bring ideas together.

exam: **Command words:** 'State' or 'name' needs one word or phrase (1 mark). 'Describe' needs the stages in order. 'Explain' needs reasons joined by 'because' or 'so'. 'Compare' needs both items with a similarity or difference.
**1-mark questions:** name the stage (e.g. 'nebula', 'protostar', 'supernova', 'white dwarf') or state what fusion is. Give one precise word, not a sentence.
**2-mark 'explain stable':** 'the **inward force of gravity** is equal to the **outward pressure** from the energy released by fusion, so the star does not shrink or expand.'

**3-mark 'how a star forms':** 'a **nebula** (cloud of dust and gas) is pulled together by **gravity**; the material heats up as it contracts to form a **protostar**; when it is hot enough, **fusion** starts and it becomes a main sequence star.'
**4-mark 'describe life cycle of the Sun':** nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf, black dwarf, and say which stage is longest.

**6-mark 'compare Sun and a much more massive star':** same start (nebula, protostar, main sequence), then the branching: red giant vs red supergiant, white dwarf/black dwarf vs supernova/neutron star or black hole. Link to mass and gravity.
**Origin of elements:** write that fusion in stars makes elements up to iron, supernovae make heavier elements and distribute them. Use the word 'distribute' or 'scatter'.
**Flow-chart questions:** fill in order, check that arrows follow the route for the given mass.
**Calculation tip:** convert km to m if needed and use speed = distance / time with c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s; give answer in seconds and minutes if asked.
**Avoid** vague words such as 'dies' or 'burns out'. Use 'fuel runs out', 'fusion', 'collapses', 'explodes as a supernova'.
**Spell** key terms correctly: supernova, protostar, nebula, equilibrium.

mistakes.r: Stars **fuse** hydrogen nuclei into helium by nuclear fusion; burning is a chemical reaction with oxygen.
The Sun is not massive enough: it will become a red giant, then a white dwarf, then a black dwarf.
mistakes.w: The Sun will explode as a supernova or become a black hole.

mistakes.r: Stars are powered by nuclear fusion (joining of light nuclei); fission is the splitting of large nuclei.
It is stable because the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure produced by fusion energy.
mistakes.w: The star is stable because it is not using fuel.

mistakes.r: A red giant is a late stage; it then becomes a white dwarf and finally a black dwarf.
mistakes.w: A red giant is the final stage.

mistakes.r: Only the most massive stars leave black holes; Sun-sized stars end as white dwarfs.
mistakes.w: All stars end as black holes.

mistakes.r: They reflect light from the Sun; only stars make their own light by fusion.
mistakes.w: Planets and moons give out their own light.

mistakes.r: Elements heavier than iron are made in the extreme conditions of a supernova.
mistakes.w: Elements heavier than iron are made in the Sun.

mistakes.r: A protostar is formed when gravity pulls dust and gas together; fusion begins afterwards.
mistakes.w: The protostar is formed by fusion.

summary: AQA 4.8.1 (Physics only) expects you to describe the Solar system and the Sun's place in the Milky Way, and to describe the life cycle of a star: how a nebula becomes a protostar and a main sequence star, and how a star the size of the Sun ends differently from a much more massive star. You must also know that fusion in stars made all the naturally occurring elements and that supernovae spread them, which links space physics to nuclear fusion and the origin of the elements.

terms.d: A very large ball of hot gas that gives out its own light and heat because of nuclear fusion in its core.
A very large group of billions of stars held together by gravity; the Sun is in the Milky Way galaxy.
The Sun and all the objects that orbit it: planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
A large body that orbits a star; the Solar system has eight planets.
A small body that orbits the Sun but is smaller than the planets, for example Pluto.
A moon: a natural object that orbits a planet.
A cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars form.
The hot, dense ball formed when a nebula is pulled together by gravity, before nuclear fusion has started.
The process in which two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, with some mass being converted into energy released as radiation.
A stable star in which the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the energy released by fusion of hydrogen into helium.
A star about the size of the Sun (or smaller) that has run out of hydrogen in its core and has expanded and cooled.
A star much more massive than the Sun that has run out of hydrogen in its core and expanded and cooled.
The small, hot, dense remnant of a Sun-sized star that no longer fuses and slowly cools.
A cold, dark remnant of a white dwarf that has cooled completely.
The enormous explosion of a massive star at the end of its life, which scatters elements into space and creates elements heavier than iron.
An extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons.
A region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape; formed from the most massive stars.
Gravity pulling inwards is balanced by outward pressure from fusion, so the star does not shrink or expand.

worked.ans: A nebula is pulled together by gravity to form a protostar. When fusion of hydrogen starts it becomes a stable main sequence star, with gravity balanced by outward pressure. When hydrogen runs out it swells into a red supergiant. Heavier elements up to iron are fused. The core then collapses and the star explodes as a supernova, scattering elements. The remaining core becomes a neutron star or a black hole.
worked.q: Describe the life cycle of a star that is much more massive than the Sun. (6 marks)
steps: Mark point 1: a **nebula**, a cloud of dust and gas, is pulled together by **gravity**.
Mark point 2: it forms a **protostar**, which heats up as it contracts.
Mark point 3: when the core is hot and dense enough, **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen into helium begins and it becomes a **main sequence star** (stable because gravity equals outward pressure).
Mark point 4: when the hydrogen runs out the star expands and cools to become a **red supergiant**, fusing heavier elements up to iron.
Mark point 5: the core collapses and the star explodes as a **supernova**, creating and scattering heavier elements.
Mark point 6: the core left behind becomes a **neutron star** or, if massive enough, a **black hole**.

worked.q: Light travels at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. The distance from the Sun to the Earth is 1.5 x 10^11 m. Calculate the time taken for light from the Sun to reach the Earth. Give your answer in seconds and in minutes. (3 marks)
steps: Rearrange speed = distance / time to give time = distance / speed.

worked.ans: The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure caused by energy released from fusion of hydrogen, so the star is in equilibrium and stable.
worked.q: Explain why a main sequence star such as the Sun stays the same size for billions of years. (3 marks)
steps: Gravity acts inwards, trying to pull the star's material together.
Fusion of hydrogen releases energy that produces an outward pressure.
These two effects are equal (equilibrium), so the star neither shrinks nor expands until the fuel runs low.
